description: Org-level testing standards: what to mock, what to assert, reproducibility, fixtures, selectors, and the user-story -> Gherkin -> test-case behaviour lifecycle that apply to every project installing AI Agile.

standards.title: Do not mock what you can hit directly
standards.description: Integration and end-to-end tests exercise the real dependency the test tier can reach, rather than a stub of it; mock doubles are reserved for pure unit tests of logic with no reachable dependency.
standards.rationale: Mocking a reachable endpoint tests the mock, not the contract.
acceptance_criteria: Integration/E2E tests in the diff call the real dependency the tier provisions rather than stubbing it.
Mock doubles introduced in the diff are confined to pure-unit tests of logic with no reachable dependency.
No diff adds a hand-rolled stub for an endpoint/service the test tier can reach directly (e.g. a real database table or service function).
anti_patterns: Mocking the real data-access client in an integration test that runs against an ephemeral database.
A fake HTTP layer standing in for a real endpoint the tier already provisions.

standards.title: Tests pin observable contracts, not implementation detail
standards.description: Tests assert observable behaviour -- status codes, response shapes, redirects, authorization outcomes -- not internal implementation. A refactor that preserves the contract must not require test changes. Do not write tests that assert framework behaviour (the UI framework, its component libraries, and data-access client libraries are trusted dependencies).
standards.rationale: Contract-first tests survive refactors and catch real regressions; implementation-coupled tests are churn.
acceptance_criteria: New tests in the diff assert observable outputs (status, response shape, redirect, authorization result), not private internals.
No test in the diff asserts behaviour owned by trusted third-party framework or client libraries.
Tests in the diff would still pass after a contract-preserving refactor of the unit under test.
anti_patterns: Asserting on a component's internal state variable instead of rendered output.
A test that re-verifies that the component library opens a dialog (framework behaviour).

standards.title: Tests are reproducible locally
standards.description: Any CI failure must reproduce locally with a documented command. Tests must not depend on CI-only state, ordering, or wall-clock; no 'only fails in CI' mysteries.
standards.rationale: Reproducibility is a testing principle; non-reproducible failures cannot be diagnosed or fixed reliably.
acceptance_criteria: New tests in the diff run deterministically given a documented local command.
Tests in the diff do not depend on execution order, ambient CI environment, or real current time without a fixed/injected clock.
Any environment a test needs is provisioned by the test or documented, not assumed to exist only in CI.
anti_patterns: A test that passes locally only because of leftover state from a previous test.
Asserting against `Date.now()` without a controlled clock.

standards.title: Each test seeds and cleans up its own fixtures; shared live data is read-only
standards.description: Every test seeds its own fixtures and either cleans them up or uses idempotent guards. Shared live data is treated as read-only and must not be mutated by a test.
standards.rationale: Self-contained fixtures keep tests isolated and re-runnable; mutating shared data causes cross-test interference and pollutes live environments.
acceptance_criteria: New tests in the diff create the data they need and remove it (or use idempotent upsert/guard) rather than relying on pre-existing rows.
No test in the diff writes to or deletes shared/live data it did not create.
Authenticated tests in the diff use the designated test identities (TEST_USER_EMAIL/TEST_USER_PASSWORD or the restricted-group/synthetic users), not arbitrary real accounts.
anti_patterns: A test that depends on a specific row already existing in a shared database.
A test that updates a shared fixture and leaves it mutated for the next test.

standards.title: Prefer stable selectors and named timeout constants
standards.description: End-to-end and component tests select elements by stable, semantic locators -- role, accessible label/placeholder, or an explicit test id -- never brittle CSS or nth-child paths. Timeout values use named constants, not inline magic numbers.
standards.rationale: Semantic locators survive markup refactors that break positional CSS selectors; named timeouts make waits legible and tunable.
acceptance_criteria: UI elements in the diff's tests are selected by role, accessible label/placeholder, or an explicit test id, not a brittle CSS/nth-child path.
Timeouts in the diff's tests use named constants, not inline magic numbers.
anti_patterns: Selecting an element by a brittle CSS/nth-child path, or hardcoding a magic-number timeout.

standards.title: Fixtures must mirror the production data shape
standards.description: Mock fixtures and test doubles return the same shape the real system returns in production; a test that passes against a fixture whose shape differs from production does not constitute evidence. When the production shape changes, fixtures are updated in the same change.
standards.rationale: A fixture that diverges from the real response shape yields green tests that hide real integration failures.
acceptance_criteria: Fixtures and test doubles in the diff return the same shape as the real production response.
When a response shape changes in the diff, the corresponding fixtures are updated in the same change.
anti_patterns: A test double returning a shape that differs from what the real system returns in production.

standards.title: Behaviour tests realise the Gherkin spec derived from the user story
standards.description: Behaviour and end-to-end tests (API and web, not pure unit tests) realise the Gherkin acceptance criteria derived from the issue's user story: user story -> Gherkin scenarios -> automated test cases. No behaviour/E2E automation is written without an approved specification, and every scenario in the approved spec is realised by a test.
standards.rationale: Anchoring automation to the approved Gherkin spec keeps tests traceable to intended behaviour and prevents tests that assert something no one specified.
acceptance_criteria: Behaviour/E2E tests in the diff realise scenarios from the issue's approved Gherkin acceptance criteria.
No behaviour/E2E test in the diff automates behaviour that has no corresponding approved scenario.
Each approved scenario touched by the diff has a realising test.
anti_patterns: Writing a behaviour/E2E test with no corresponding approved Gherkin scenario, or leaving an approved scenario with no test.

standards.title: Write idempotent CRUD/E2E tests
standards.description: CRUD and E2E tests must be idempotent so re-runs do not fail on unique-constraint violations: before creating a record, check whether it already exists (from a previous run) and, if so, verify and pass rather than re-creating. Tests clean up or use idempotent guards.
standards.rationale: The suite runs repeatedly (scheduled and on PRs) against shared environments; non-idempotent create steps fail on the second run.
acceptance_criteria: Create-flow tests in the diff check for the record's existence before creating and short-circuit to verification if present.
Tests in the diff do not assume a clean database and do not fail on re-run due to unique constraints.
Test data created in the diff is cleaned up or guarded so repeated runs stay green.
anti_patterns: A test that always creates `code = 'TEST'` and fails the second run on a unique violation.
Assuming an empty table at the start of an E2E create scenario.

standards.title: Test artefacts live in their canonical locations; the Gherkin .feature is the testable spec
standards.description: Test artefacts have a single canonical home. Behaviour specifications are Gherkin .feature files, and their automated realisations live in the project's designated test directories (web and API/service suites in their conventional locations). The .feature spec is the testable specification -- tests realise it, they do not replace it.
standards.rationale: One canonical location per artefact type keeps the suite discoverable and keeps the Gherkin spec, not ad-hoc test code, as the source of intended behaviour.
acceptance_criteria: Behaviour specs added in the diff are Gherkin .feature files in the project's designated specification location.
Automated tests in the diff live in the project's conventional test directories for their tier (web vs API/service).
anti_patterns: Placing a behaviour spec or test outside the project's designated locations, or treating ad-hoc test code as the specification instead of the .feature.

standards.title: New public behaviour requires at least one test
standards.description: Every new public function, method, class, or API endpoint introduced in a diff must have at least one corresponding test that exercises the primary success path. Untested public behaviour is not shippable.
standards.rationale: Code without tests cannot be refactored safely, cannot be verified by CI, and will silently break as the codebase evolves. The cost of writing a test at authoring time is a fraction of the cost of debugging a regression later.
acceptance_criteria: For every new public function or method in the diff, at least one test in the same diff (or an existing test file) exercises its primary happy-path behaviour.
For every new HTTP route, CLI command, or public API endpoint, at least one test asserts the expected response for a valid request.
Tests for new behaviour are added in the same PR as the behaviour — not deferred to a follow-up.
Private functions and internal helpers that are only reachable via tested public interfaces are exempt from direct test requirements.
anti_patterns: Introducing a new function and leaving the test file unchanged.
Adding a new API endpoint with only a placeholder '# TODO: add tests' comment.
Implementing a new feature and planning to 'add tests in the next PR'.
Marking a function as private solely to avoid the test requirement when it has externally observable effects.

standards.title: Unit tests must not make real network or filesystem calls
standards.description: Tests in the unit-test layer must not perform real HTTP requests, DNS lookups, database queries, or filesystem writes outside a designated temp directory. All I/O must be replaced by mocks, fakes, or fixtures injected at test setup.
standards.rationale: Tests that rely on real external state are non-deterministic, slow, and fail in CI environments without network access. They also create hidden dependencies between tests and external systems that are hard to reproduce on failure.
acceptance_criteria: No test in the unit-test layer makes an outbound HTTP request (requests.get, urllib, httpx, fetch) without mocking the transport layer.
No test reads from or writes to paths outside of tempfile.mkdtemp(), pytest's tmp_path, or an equivalent isolated temporary directory.
No test opens a real database connection — database calls are replaced by in-memory databases (sqlite :memory:), fakes, or mock objects.
Network or filesystem mocking is applied at the lowest practical boundary (e.g. patching the HTTP adapter, not the entire requests module).
Integration tests that intentionally exercise real I/O are placed in a separate directory (tests/integration/) and excluded from the default pytest run.
anti_patterns: A unit test that calls requests.get('https://api.example.com/...') without patching.
A test that writes to a hardcoded path like /tmp/test_output.json that could collide across parallel test runs.
Mocking an entire external library (mock.patch('requests')) instead of patching at the HTTP adapter boundary.
A test that passes only when a specific database server is reachable, with no skip or xfail guard.

standards.title: Each test asserts exactly one behaviour
standards.description: Each test function must assert a single, named behaviour. Tests must not be assertion-free, and must not bundle multiple unrelated scenarios into one test body.
standards.rationale: Tests that verify multiple behaviours produce ambiguous failure messages — a reader cannot tell which behaviour broke. Assertion-free tests always pass, giving false confidence. One behaviour per test makes failures self-documenting.
acceptance_criteria: Every test function in the diff contains at least one explicit assertion (assert, pytest.raises, unittest assertion method).

Each test function asserts a single logical behaviour — multiple assertions are permitted only when they collectively verify one indivisible outcome (e.g. asserting both status code and response body for one request).
Test functions that verify multiple distinct scenarios (happy path AND error path) are split into separate test functions.
No test uses a bare pass or returns early without asserting anything.
anti_patterns: A test named test_user_flow that exercises login, update, and logout in sequence with assertions scattered throughout.
A test function with zero assert statements (assertion-free test).
A parametrized test where some parameter combinations test happy paths and others test error paths in the same assertion block.
Using a loop to run multiple independent scenarios inside a single test function.

standards.title: Test names encode scenario and expected outcome
standards.description: Test function names must describe the condition under test and the expected outcome in a form that reads as a specification. Names must not be generic (test_1, test_it, test_works) or repeat only the function name being tested.
standards.rationale: A test name is the first and often only information a developer sees when a test fails in CI. A descriptive name eliminates the need to read the test body to understand what broke and what the expected behaviour was.
acceptance_criteria: Every test function name in the diff follows the pattern test_<scenario>_<expected_outcome> or a domain-appropriate equivalent that encodes both the condition and the result.
No test function is named test_<function_name> with no further qualification (e.g. test_parse, test_send).
No test function is named with a numeric suffix (test_1, test_case_2) as the only differentiator.
Class-based test suites name the class after the unit under test (TestClassName) and name methods after the behaviour (test_raises_when_input_is_empty).
anti_patterns: def test_1(), def test_2() for two related cases.
def test_parse() with no description of what input or what outcome is expected.
def test_it_works() — too vague to diagnose on failure.
def test_user() when the test actually verifies that creating a user with a duplicate email raises ValueError.

standards.title: New behaviour tests cover the primary error path, not just the happy path
standards.description: Every new or materially changed function, method, class, or API endpoint that has a defined error condition (a duplicate/conflict case, a not-found case, or another documented failure mode) must have at least one test exercising that error path, in addition to the happy-path test required by STD-TEST-011. A behaviour is not considered tested when only its success case is verified.
standards.rationale: The happy path is the easiest case to get right and the least likely to regress silently; the error path -- rejecting a duplicate, handling a missing resource -- is where defects hide and where a missed test lets a regression ship. Requiring both closes the most common gap between 'passes CI' and 'actually correct'.
acceptance_criteria: For every new or changed function/method/class/endpoint in the diff that has a documented duplicate/conflict condition, at least one test asserts the expected error behaviour when that condition is triggered.
For every new or changed function/method/class/endpoint in the diff that has a documented not-found condition, at least one test asserts the expected error behaviour when the target does not exist.
Error-path tests assert the specific observable outcome (status code, exception type, error message shape) -- not merely that 'something' was raised.
Error-path tests are added in the same PR as the behaviour, per STD-TEST-011's same-PR requirement.
anti_patterns: A new 'create X' endpoint with a test for successful creation but no test for the duplicate-key rejection path.
A new 'get X by id' function with a happy-path test but no test asserting the not-found behaviour.
A try/except in the implementation with no test ever triggering the except branch.
